issues.detail: Code snippets are illustrative skeletons that cannot run as-is: Agent, _classify, and the _check_* quality-gate methods are undefined, and no LLM client is wired in.
The three examples are one-paragraph prompts with no sample inputs, outputs, or walkthrough of the resulting agent interactions, so they are less realistic than concrete demonstrations.

scenarios.name: code-review-pipeline-with-retry-gate
scenarios.rationale: Both deliver an orchestrator with deduplication and severity ranking, a bounded 3-attempt retry and a quality gate that rejects bad output. B is runnable code with backoff, though only on infrastructure errors, and a coverage check. A has no backoff and no blocking-versus-warning distinction, and it wasn't written to disk or run, though the code is inline. B also lacks the blocking/warning distinction.

scenarios.name: support-ticket-router-with-fallback
scenarios.rationale: B matches the rubric directly: an LLM router returns JSON with agent, confidence and reasoning, falls back to a generalist when confidence is below 0.7 or the agent name is unregistered, and builds a name-to-agent registry whose descriptions go into the routing prompt. A uses a different design with per-category thresholds, a margin check, a triage queue and a tool-call classifier that returns probabilities. It has no agent/confidence/reasoning JSON, no 0.7 gate, no registry-name validation and no descriptions in the prompt, so it only partly meets the intent of low-confidence safety.

scenarios.name: research-swarm-shared-memory-parallel
scenarios.rationale: Both run the four agents concurrently with asyncio.gather, share a Board with agent attribution, enforce a budget cap, and treat pages as untrusted with quote verification; A uses forced tool-call JSON schemas for inter-agent validation, so it meets the structured-validation requirement more fully, while B relies on parsing free-text JSON, has stubbed search backends, and adds a call cap, a weaker regex filter, and merged corroboration.
